Where is tomorrows talent coming from?

If AI takes on more of the work juniors learn from, how do they build the judgement we expect from senior hires?
For fund management firms and senior leaders across legal and compliance, that question is worth asking now.

In law practice, where many of the inhouse lawyers come from, early stage document review, research and first drafts serve two purposes; they get the work done, and they give junior lawyers experience. Reviewing a document, missing something and understanding a senior associates or partners correction are all part of learning.

As more of that work has becomes AI led, where is the opportunity to cut their teeth?
If the hierarchy in law practice was rejigged for AI to do first review and associates over see the AI, fairly well constructed but incorrect points, may get missed.  
If that review moves straight to senior lawyers, where does the junior gain the experience.

In fund management compliance, the challenge is similar, but there is no direct entry route like a training contract.
Compliance monitoring, routine business queries and process driven work can give junior compliance officers, exposure to how a fund operates, engagement with senior stakeholders and refined knowledge on FCA rules.
If firms automate more of those tasks and reduce entry-level hiring, the consequences could extend well beyond today’s team.

Less investment in that key development, across both role types would result in a much narrower pool of subject matter experts in the future.  Firms that invest in early stage talent now, could reap the benefits in years to come.  Small talent pools and lack of practical knowledge in private markets was a problem they faced not long ago, its probably not something we want to regress back to.

Last week, I spent two days at AI SUMMIT BARCELONA  and the conversation I keep coming back to wasnt about a model, a framework or a use case.

The traditional job has been dying since 1994.

Some notable “deaths” include:

- Finding work through apps
- Taking on small tasks online

Here’s the reality:

80% firm z listy Global 500. Tyle - według prognozy Gartnera z 15 września - do 2030 roku wpisze w umowę ze swoim CIO lub CAIO nową rolę: „Evidence Custodian". Osoba, która potrafi udowodnić, jak i dlaczego AI podjęła konkretną decyzję.

Czytam to jako koniec pewnej epoki: polityk AI pisanych na półkę. I początek czegoś, co każdy zarząd zna z własnego doświadczenia - za decyzję odpowiada się nie intencją, tylko udokumentowanym działaniem.

Ciekawy jest też drugi wątek tej samej prognozy: to ubezpieczyciele, nie regulatorzy, mają do 2030 roku kształtować governance AI - przez warunki polis od odpowiedzialności. Udokumentowane działanie przestaje być kwestią zgodności. Staje się kwestią wysokości składki.

Dla firm w Polsce i CEE to raczej szansa niż obowiązek. Jeśli agent AI już dziś wspiera decyzje kredytowe, rekrutacyjne czy cenowe, to firmy, które potrafią odtworzyć „dlaczego padła taka, a nie inna", będą miały przewagę - w rozmowie z klientem, audytorem i ubezpieczycielem.

Governance powoli przestaje być slajdem w prezentacji. Staje się linią w umowie.

Przez 20 lat pracy z zarządami widziałem wiele transformacji, w których odpowiedzialność za technologię była rozproszona tak skutecznie, że nie miał jej nikt. Teraz ktoś z imienia i nazwiska weźmie ją kontraktowo. Zaskakująco prosty pomysł - dziwne, że trzeba było AI, żeby na niego wpaść. 😉

[Eng]
80% of Global 500 companies. That's how many - according to Gartner's 15 September forecast - will by 2030 write a new role into their CIO's or CAIO's contract: "Evidence Custodian". The person able to prove how and why AI made a specific decision.

I read it as the end of an era: AI policies written for the shelf. And the start of something every board knows from experience - you answer for a decision not with intentions, but with documented action.

The second thread of the same forecast is just as interesting: by 2030, insurers - not regulators - are expected to shape AI governance, through liability policy terms. Documented action stops being a compliance matter. It becomes a matter of the premium.

For companies in Poland and CEE this is more an opportunity than an obligation. If an AI agent already supports credit, hiring or pricing decisions, the firms able to reconstruct "why this one and not another" will have the edge - with clients, auditors and insurers alike.

Governance is slowly ceasing to be a slide in a deck. It's becoming a line in a contract.

In 20 years of working with boards I've seen many transformations where accountability for technology was spread so effectively that nobody had it. Now someone, by name, will take it contractually. A surprisingly simple idea - strange it took AI to get us there. 😉

I think a lot of AI startups are going to die for a very boring reason.

They built something that can do 47 things.

Nobody urgently needed any of them.
There’s been a weird race to build “AI for businesses.”

AI that writes.
AI that researches.
AI that automates.
AI that helps teams “work smarter.”
Cool.

But who is actually desperate enough to pay for it?
The AI products I find most interesting aren't trying to be useful to everyone.
They're painfully specific.

AI for lawyers.
AI for accountants.
AI for sales teams.
AI for compliance.

AI for one very annoying workflow that currently costs someone 20 hours a week.
That's where the real opportunity is.
Because people don't really buy AI.

They buy outcomes.
A lawyer doesn't wake up thinking:
“I need some AI today.”
They think:
“I need to review 300 contracts without hiring another person.”
That's a much better business.

And I think this matters even more in Africa.
There are thousands of incredibly specific problems sitting inside African businesses that nobody has built properly for yet.

Tax.
Compliance.
Payroll.
Cross-border payments.
Import/export.
Licensing.
Healthcare administration.
The list is ridiculous.

You don't necessarily need another “AI platform for African businesses.”
Maybe you just need to find one extremely painful problem and become ridiculously good at solving it.

The interesting question isn't:
“Where can we add AI?”
It's:
“What problem is painful enough that people will pay us to make it disappear?”
That's where I'd start.

Remote jobs are not gone. You are just searching the wrong words.

I use Perplexity to uncover global remote roles that most standard filters never surface.

Many companies don’t write:
“work from anywhere”

Instead, they describe it with terms like:
• contract
• freelance
• global team
• work across time zones
• anywhere
• outside the US
• remote in selected countries

That tiny wording shift makes a big difference.

Here is the simple workflow:

1/ Search for hiring signals
In Perplexity, prompt:

“Find companies hiring for [your role] that may accept people from many countries. Look for words like contract, freelance, global team, work across time zones, anywhere, or outside the US. Skip jobs that clearly need US-only hiring. Show me the company, job link, country limits, job type, and why it may fit.”

Now you’re not just searching for “remote.”
You’re searching the language companies actually use.

2/ Check the company pages
Then ask:

“Check company career pages, founder posts, and hiring pages for this role. Find companies that look open to global remote workers, even if the job title does not say work from anywhere.”

This is how you catch roles that filters skip.

3/ Save the good ones
Drop the results into Notion or Google Sheets.

Track:
• company
• role
• link
• country limit
• time zone need
• job type
• notes

4/ Match your CV to that kind of job
Use ChatGPT or Claude.
Ask it to rewrite your strongest CV points to emphasize:
• working alone
• clear writing
• fast work
• working with people in different time zones
• real results

The best global remote jobs are often not inside the “remote” filter.
They’re sitting behind simple words.

AI helps you spot them faster.

Every AI assistant is good at something. The trick is giving it the right job.
Here's who we'd hire for what.

ChatGPT gets the all-rounder role. It covers the widest range of tasks, it's strong on complex coding, and its deep research mode builds detailed reports from multiple sources.

Claude gets the writing. It handles nuance well and reasons across long documents, which suits contracts, specifications and policy work.
Google Gemini gets the job if your business runs on Google Workspace. It works inside Docs and Gmail and includes built-in image and video generation.

Microsoft Copilot gets the job if you run on Windows and Microsoft 365. It sits inside Outlook, Teams, Word and Excel, the tools your team already opens every morning.

Notice something about the last two. They're chosen largely for where they live, not what they do.

That's often the real decision. The best assistant is usually the one that fits the systems your people already use, because that's the one they'll actually use.

Hiring the tool is the easy part. Knowing which processes to point it at, and which ones to leave alone, is where the value sits.

The best acquisition target may be the company nobody has put on your list yet.

And AI is getting very good at finding it.

For years, M&A origination has relied heavily on networks, databases, advisors, sector knowledge and a lot of manual research.

All still extremely valuable.
But AI is adding another layer.

Imagine an agent continuously scanning thousands of companies, websites, financial signals, management changes, hiring patterns, patents, customer reviews and market movements.

Not simply looking for companies for sale.
Looking for companies that fit a specific investment thesis.
Then comes due diligence.

A data room containing thousands of contracts, financial documents, corporate records and operational files can increasingly be analysed, classified and cross-checked automatically. The interesting part isn't just speed.

It's the ability to ask questions across the entire deal:
Where are the anomalies?
What doesn't match?
Which contracts create concentration risk?
Where could the investment thesis fail?
And after that, another step.

AI can help model different post-acquisition scenarios: synergies, integration costs, revenue assumptions, organizational overlaps and potential risks.

Suddenly, the traditional M&A workflow starts looking very different:
Source → Screen → Analyse → Challenge → Simulate → Decide.

AI can increasingly support almost everything before that final word.
Decide.
And that's where I think the human role actually becomes more important.
Because I've been involved in acquisitions where spreadsheets told one story and walking into the company told another.

You can analyse the numbers.
You can analyse the contracts.
You can analyse the market.

But understanding the entrepreneur sitting opposite you, the management team, the culture and whether two organizations will actually work together is much harder to put into an algorithm.

So perhaps AI won't replace M&A professionals.

It may simply remove a huge amount of work that prevented them from doing the part that matters most:
judgement.

The question is no longer whether AI will enter the deal room.
It's what we'll do differently once it's sitting at the table.

I spent part of this week looking at remote engineering roles advertised in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, UK and US.

The first thing that jumped out: on the first few pages of results, most of the "employers" weren't employers. They were talent marketplaces and staffing firms advertising roles on someone else's behalf.

The companies actually hiring were harder to find. When I did find them, three patterns stood out:

1. The roles are specialist. Platform engineers, ServiceNow leads, data engineers for ML teams, technical PMs for fintech builds.
2. Many are project-shaped. Time-boxed contracts, one product, a defined build.
3. Volume isn't the problem. Several had over 100 applicants within a day of posting. Finding the right person in that pile is the hard part.

That's the gap Resquad AI is built for. Instead of another job post, we match the requirement against verified engineers from 1,200+ vetted agencies and send a shortlist within 48 hours.

If you have a remote role or project team that's been open longer than you'd like, send me the JD/scope and I'll tell you whether we can fill it.

Bigger #AI Isn't Always Better. #Smarter Allocation Is.

Imagine hiring a heart surgeon to put on a Band-Aid.

Technically capable. Ridiculously expensive.

For years, the AI industry has followed a similar logic: use the biggest model, the most powerful chip and the maximum computing power available.

In 2026, the more interesting question is: how much #intelligence does this task actually need?

Three shifts are bringing that question to the forefront.

1. AI ROUTERS: Pick the right model.

Not every task needs a frontier AI model.

Summarising an email? A smaller, cheaper model may suffice.

Analysing a complex legal contract? Bring in the heavyweight.

AI routers act like smart dispatchers, directing each request to a suitable model based on cost, capability and latency.

Platforms such as #OpenRouter and #Vercel AI Gateway are built around this routing approach.

The goal: get the required answer without paying for unnecessary capability.

2. MIXTURE OF EXPERTS (#MoE): Pick the right part of the model.

Now take the same idea *inside* a single AI model.

Imagine a hospital with specialists in cardiology, neurology and orthopaedics.

Every patient doesn't need every specialist.

MoE models work similarly. An internal routing mechanism activates selected expert networks for a given input, rather than engaging every part of the model.

The result? A model can have a large pool of learned knowledge while using only a fraction of its parameters for each task.

More capacity doesn't have to mean activating everything, every time.

3. CPU-BASED INFERENCE: Do you always need expensive #GPUs?

The efficiency question extends to hardware, too.

GPUs are excellent at many AI workloads, but not every inference task requires a specialised GPU cluster.

For some workloads, existing #CPUs may offer a more economical option, depending on performance, latency and scale.

Kompact AI is among the companies exploring this approach.

The point isn't that GPUs are obsolete. It's that **the most powerful hardware isn't automatically the most economical choice.

The bigger picture

Look at the pattern:

→ AI routers select the right model.
→ MoE activates the relevant experts within a model.
→ Hardware optimisation matches computing resources to the workload.

Three different layers. One underlying principle:

Stop paying for capability you don't need.

The first phase of the AI race was about making models bigger and more capable.

The next phase may increasingly reward those who deliver the required intelligence with less compute, lower costs and better energy efficiency.

Because in business, the winner isn't necessarily the one using the biggest machine.

It's the one that gets the job done at the right cost.

Perhaps AI's next breakthrough isn't simply more intelligence. It's making intelligence economical.

📉 IS GENERATIVE AI BECOMING A THREAT TO INDIA'S IT GIANTS?

For decades, companies like Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, and Wipro built their business models around one thing: people.
More projects.
More engineers.
More billable hours.
But AI is changing that equation faster than anyone expected.

Over the past year, India's largest IT stocks have witnessed a significant correction, with investors increasingly questioning how Generative AI and autonomous AI agents could reshape the industry's future.
📊 The numbers are hard to ignore:
🔻 Wipro fell nearly 36.7%
🔻 Infosys dropped 35.8%
🔻 TCS declined 31.6%

At the same time, global brokerages have warned of continued pressure on margins as enterprises rethink traditional outsourcing contracts.
The concern isn't that AI will replace entire companies.
The concern is that AI is replacing parts of the work these companies have historically monetized.
Tasks such as:
• Code generation
• Software testing
• Documentation
• Bug fixing
• Process automation
• Customer support workflows
can now be completed faster and with fewer human resources than before.

This is forcing a massive shift from the traditional "effort-based billing" model toward an AI-powered productivity model.
And investors are watching closely.
👨‍💻 The workforce impact is already becoming visible.

Reports indicate major restructuring across the IT sector, with companies focusing more aggressively on:
✅ AI engineering
✅ Agentic AI development
✅ Cloud infrastructure
✅ Enterprise automation
✅ Data and model operations
while reducing dependence on large entry-level hiring pipelines.

The challenge for India's IT giants isn't whether AI will arrive.
It's whether they can transform themselves quickly enough to stay ahead of it.
The companies that successfully evolve from outsourcing partners into AI transformation partners could emerge stronger than ever.

The ones that don't may face growing pressure in a world where software increasingly writes software.
The next decade may become the biggest transformation in Indian IT history.
And we're already watching the first chapter unfold.

👇 Do you think Generative AI will ultimately help companies like Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, and Wipro grow faster—or will it permanently disrupt the traditional IT services model?
